summary.text: A submarine canyon is a steep-sided valley cut into the seabed of the continental slope, sometimes reaching well onto the continental shelf.
The main force carving them is thought to be turbidity currents, dense flows of sediment-laden water, together with underwater landslides.
There are an estimated 9,477 submarine canyons on Earth, covering about 11% of the continental slope.

facts.label: Tallest walls
facts.value: Up to 5 km, in the Great Bahama Canyon

facts.label: Deep example
facts.value: Avilés Canyon off Spain, about 4,700 m deep

facts.label: Ancient examples
facts.value: Found in rocks from the Neoproterozoic

items.prompt: An early idea held that rivers carved these canyons during ice ages, when sea level was lower. Why can't that explain most of them?

options.label: No rivers flowed at all during ice ages
Canyons are always found far from rivers
Canyons reach far deeper than sea level ever fell
River water cannot erode solid rock

items.explain: Canyons have been mapped as deep as 3,000 m, and sea level is well established never to have fallen that far, so river erosion in open air cannot have cut them.

items.prompt: How fast can a turbidity current race down a submarine canyon?
items.explain: Turbidity currents travel downslope at great speed, as much as 70 km/h (43 mph).

items.prompt: Some extra-deep canyons near the Mediterranean were cut far below today's sea level. What allowed rivers like the Nile to carve so deep?

options.label: Glaciers dug the channels before melting
Volcanic eruptions blasted the valleys open
A meteor impact cracked the seabed
The sea was cut off and evaporated, exposing its bed

items.explain: Five to six million years ago the Mediterranean was isolated from the Atlantic and dried up, so rivers could cut deep into the exposed bed before the basin flooded again.

items.prompt: Where would you expect submarine canyons to be steeper, shorter and more closely packed together?
items.explain: Canyons are more common on the steep slopes of active margins, and there they are steeper, shorter, more branching and more closely spaced than on passive margins.

items.prompt: On land, canyons channel flowing river water. What do submarine canyons channel across the seafloor?

options.label: Warm currents from the ocean surface

items.explain: Submarine canyons serve as channels for turbidity currents, which are dense flows of water loaded with sediment.

items.prompt: A turbidity current rushes down a canyon, eroding the slope as it goes. Where does it finally drop its load of sediment?

options.label: On the beach where it began
On top of the continental shelf

items.explain: Turbidity currents erode the continental slope and finally deposit their sediment onto the abyssal plain, where the particles settle out.

paragraphs.heading: Valleys under the sea
paragraphs.text: A submarine canyon is a valley with steep sides, carved into the seabed of the continental slope, sometimes reaching well onto the continental shelf. Its walls are nearly vertical, and in the Great Bahama Canyon they stand up to 5 km from floor to rim. There are an estimated 9,477 of them on Earth, covering about 11% of the continental slope. Many lie more than 2 km below sea level, and Avilés Canyon, off Asturias in Spain, reaches about 4,700 m.

paragraphs.heading: Channels for turbidity currents
paragraphs.text: Canyons on land carry water across the land, and submarine canyons do the same job for turbidity currents on the seafloor. A turbidity current is a flow of dense water loaded with sediment, fed by rivers or stirred up on the seabed by storms, landslides, earthquakes and other disturbances. These flows rush downslope at up to 70 km/h, wearing away the slope and finally dropping their load on the abyssal plain. Deposits called turbidites pile up at the canyon mouths and build an abyssal fan.

paragraphs.heading: Where canyons begin
paragraphs.text: About 3% of canyons include shelf valleys cut right across the shelf, with their upper ends lined up with, or even inside, the mouths of big rivers; examples include the Congo River and the Hudson Canyon. About 28.5% cut back into the edge of the shelf. Most, about 68.5%, begin on the slope below the shelf edge and never cut far across the shelf. Some run seaward across shelves for hundreds of kilometres before they reach the abyssal plain.

paragraphs.heading: Active and passive margins
paragraphs.text: Canyons are more common on the steep slopes of active margins than on the gentler slopes of passive margins. On active margins they are also steeper, shorter and more closely spaced. They cut through every kind of material, from loose sediment to crystalline rock, and their walls wear back through bioerosion or slumping. Ancient canyons have even been found in rocks from the Neoproterozoic.

paragraphs.heading: An old puzzle
paragraphs.text: What carves these canyons has been argued over since the early 1930s. An early, obvious idea was that rivers cut them in glacial times, when the sea stood about 125 meters lower and rivers flowed out to the shelf edge. But canyons have been mapped as deep as 3,000 meters, and many lines of evidence show the sea never dropped that far, so rivers in open air cannot explain them. Today the main tools are thought to be turbidity currents and underwater landslides, with turbidity or density currents as major players.

paragraphs.heading: How slopes fail
paragraphs.text: A turbidity current can start when sediment dumped quickly on the upper slope becomes unstable and gives way, perhaps triggered by an earthquake. Canyons also show other slope failures. Mass wasting is the slower, smaller movement of material downhill, slumping is the rotation of masses on a slope, and landslides tear loose and move whole masses of sediment. Many of these processes act to different degrees in different places, even within one canyon at different times.

paragraphs.heading: A sea that dried up
paragraphs.text: Some very deep canyons formed another way. When a sea whose bed lies far below sea level is cut off from the ocean, it can dry up, quickly if the climate is arid, and rivers flowing in can then cut deep into the bare bed. In the Messinian salinity crisis, five to six million years ago, the Mediterranean was cut off from the Atlantic and evaporated in roughly a thousand years. The Nile delta and other rivers pushed far beyond where they are now, and after a cataclysmic flood refilled the basin, the canyons they had cut were left far below today's sea level.
